questions.q: An HIV-infected person is diagnosed as having AIDS when the helper T (CD4) cell count falls below about:
questions.x: A normal CD4 count is roughly 500–1500 cells per mm³. When it falls below about 200 per mm³, immunity is so weak that AIDS is diagnosed.

questions.q: In many developing countries, including Pakistan, the most common serious bacterial opportunistic infection in people with AIDS is:
questions.x: Weak cell-mediated immunity lets Mycobacterium tuberculosis become active, so tuberculosis is the leading opportunistic infection in AIDS patients in such countries.

questions.q: In mitochondria, the ATP synthase enzymes are found in the:
o: Stalked particles (F1 particles) on the inner membrane
questions.x: ATP synthase forms the stalked (F1, elementary) particles projecting from the inner membrane and cristae into the matrix. Protons flowing through them drive ATP formation.

questions.q: Germinating seeds release 70 cm³ of carbon dioxide while taking in 100 cm³ of oxygen. The main substrate being respired is most likely:
questions.x: RQ = 70 ÷ 100 = 0.7, the typical value for fat (as in oily seeds). Carbohydrate gives 1.0, and anaerobic respiration or organic acids give values above 1.

questions.q: The word 'glycolysis' literally means:
questions.x: Glyco = sugar and lysis = splitting. In glycolysis one six-carbon glucose is split into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules.

questions.q: If the DNA double helix is compared to a twisted ladder, the rungs of the ladder are:
o: Base pairs held by hydrogen bonds
questions.x: The two sugar–phosphate backbones form the sides of the ladder, and the paired bases joined by hydrogen bonds form the rungs.

questions.q: A tRNA anticodon, written 3'→5', is CCG. The DNA template triplet for the matching mRNA codon, also written 3'→5', is:
questions.x: Anticodon 3'-CCG-5' pairs with the codon 5'-GGC-3'. That codon was copied from the template 3'-CCG-5', so the template has the same bases as the anticodon in the same direction. 3'-GGC-5' would be the codon's bases, and DNA never contains U.

questions.q: Before an amino acid can be added to a polypeptide, it is attached to its own tRNA. This step needs:
o: A specific activating enzyme and energy from ATP
Only hydrogen bonding with the anticodon
The ribosome and a stop codon
RNA polymerase and a DNA template
questions.x: An amino acid-activating enzyme (aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase) attaches each amino acid to its correct tRNA, using energy from ATP. The anticodon is not involved in this step.

questions.q: If ice were denser than liquid water, what would happen to a pond in a very cold winter?
o: Ice would sink, so the pond could freeze solid from the bottom up and its animals could die
Ice would float as usual and insulate the water below
The pond would never freeze at any temperature
Only the surface would freeze, keeping the bottom at 4 °C
questions.x: In reality ice floats and insulates the water beneath. If ice sank, new ice would keep forming at the surface and sinking, so the pond could freeze right through.

questions.q: When iodine solution is added to glycogen, the colour produced is:
o: Deep purple with a brick-red precipitate
questions.x: Glycogen gives a red or reddish-brown colour with iodine. Starch gives a blue-black colour, and a brick-red precipitate is the result of Benedict's test for reducing sugars.

questions.q: Which lipoprotein carries most of the cholesterol from the liver to the body tissues?
questions.x: LDL delivers cholesterol to body cells, which is why a high LDL level raises the risk of deposits in arteries. HDL carries cholesterol the other way, back to the liver.

questions.q: Casein, the main protein of milk, is a conjugated protein that contains:
o: Haem groups, making it a chromoprotein
Nucleic acid, making it a nucleoprotein
Phosphate groups, making it a phosphoprotein
questions.x: Casein carries phosphate groups attached to its amino acids, so it is a phosphoprotein. These phosphate groups help it bind calcium in milk.

questions.q: In the small intestine, water acts as a reagent when fats are hydrolysed. The products of this hydrolysis are:
questions.x: Lipase uses water to break the ester bonds of fats, giving fatty acids and glycerol. Amino acids come from proteins, glucose and fructose from sucrose, and nucleotides from nucleic acids.

questions.q: Starch, glycogen and cellulose are all polymers of the same monomer, which is:
questions.x: All three polysaccharides are made only of glucose units; they differ in the form of glucose (alpha or beta), the bonds and the branching. Maltose is a disaccharide, not a monomer.

questions.q: Which set of nitrogenous bases is common to both DNA and RNA?
questions.x: Adenine, guanine and cytosine occur in both nucleic acids. Thymine is found only in DNA and uracil only in RNA.

questions.q: Lipoproteins such as HDL and LDL are found mainly in:
questions.x: HDL and LDL are plasma lipoproteins that carry cholesterol and other lipids in the blood.

questions.q: The Golgi apparatus is made of a stack of:
questions.x: Each Golgi body (dictyosome) is a stack of flattened cisternae with vesicles at their edges. Cristae belong to mitochondria and thylakoids to chloroplasts.

questions.q: Cytoplasmic streaming and membrane-bound organelles are features of:
questions.x: Eukaryotic cytoplasm streams and contains membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotic cells show no cytoplasmic streaming and have no such organelles.

questions.q: A palisade cell of a leaf contains an organelle that a liver cell does not. This organelle is the:
questions.x: Chloroplasts are found only in photosynthetic cells such as leaf palisade cells. Mitochondria, Golgi apparatus and ribosomes occur in both.

questions.q: The outer and inner membranes of a mitochondrion differ in that:
o: The outer membrane is folded into cristae
The inner membrane carries ribosomes on its outer surface
The outer membrane is smooth and more permeable, while the inner one is folded and less permeable
Only the outer membrane contains proteins
questions.x: The outer membrane is smooth and has pores that let small molecules through; the inner membrane is folded into cristae and controls movement of materials tightly.

questions.q: A second strong stimulus is applied to a point on an axon while the first action potential there is still at its peak. The second stimulus:
o: Immediately produces a second action potential of the same size
Makes the first impulse travel backwards
Produces no new action potential, because that region is in the absolute refractory period
questions.x: During the absolute refractory period no stimulus, however strong, can start another action potential, because the Na+ channels cannot reopen yet.

questions.q: In the blinking reflex that follows a touch on the cornea, the effector is the:
questions.x: The response is closing of the eyelid, so the effector is the eyelid muscle. The corneal nerve endings are the receptors, and the iris muscle is the effector of the pupil reflex, not of blinking.

questions.q: Only the interneurons in one segment of the spinal cord are destroyed; sensory and motor neurons survive. Which reflex of that segment would still work?
o: A stretch reflex such as a tendon jerk
A withdrawal reflex from a painful stimulus
None of the reflexes of that segment
questions.x: Stretch reflexes are monosynaptic: the sensory neuron synapses directly with the motor neuron, so no interneuron is needed. Withdrawal reflexes depend on interneurons and would fail.

questions.q: The term 'nerve fibre' refers to:
o: A single axon or long dendrite with its covering sheaths
A bundle of many axons wrapped in connective tissue
The cell body of a neuron with its nucleus
A group of cell bodies outside the CNS
questions.x: A nerve fibre is one long neuron process with its sheaths. A bundle of fibres is a nerve, and a group of cell bodies outside the CNS is a ganglion.

questions.q: The Na+ channels that open when the axon membrane is depolarised to threshold are called:
questions.x: These channels open in response to a change in membrane voltage. Ligand-gated channels open when a chemical such as a neurotransmitter binds.

questions.q: Which receptor is correctly paired with its location?
o: Olfactory receptor cells – roof of the nasal cavity
Pacinian corpuscles – outer layer of the epidermis
questions.x: Olfactory cells lie in the epithelium at the roof of the nasal cavity. Pacinian corpuscles are deep in the dermis, taste cells are in taste buds and rods and cones are in the retina.

questions.q: Which reflex is polysynaptic?
o: Withdrawing the foot after stepping on a thorn
The stretch reflex of the calf muscle
questions.x: Withdrawal reflexes have at least one interneuron between the sensory and motor neurons, so they are polysynaptic. The knee jerk, ankle jerk and other stretch reflexes are monosynaptic.

questions.q: A single action potential at one point of an axon lasts about:
questions.x: Depolarisation and repolarisation together take only about one to two milliseconds at any one point of the membrane.

questions.q: Two enzymes each need an organic cofactor. After dialysis, which removes small molecules, enzyme X loses its activity but enzyme Y does not. The most likely explanation is that:
o: X has a prosthetic group, while Y uses a coenzyme
X uses a coenzyme, while Y has a prosthetic group
Both have tightly bound prosthetic groups
questions.x: A coenzyme is loosely attached and is removed by dialysis, leaving an inactive apoenzyme. A prosthetic group is tightly bound and stays with the enzyme.

questions.q: The amino acids that make up an enzyme's active site:
o: Always lie next to each other in the chain
Are found only at the two ends of the chain
Are often far apart in the polypeptide chain but are brought together by folding
Are all the same amino acid
questions.x: The active site is formed by the three-dimensional folding of the chain, so amino acids from distant parts of the sequence come together to form it.

questions.q: The lock-and-key model is most useful in explaining:
o: Why enzymes are denatured by heat
Why the active site changes shape during binding
Why an enzyme acts on only one specific substrate
questions.x: In this model a rigid active site fits only one exactly matching substrate, just as one lock fits one key. Shape change on binding is the idea of induced fit.

questions.q: An enzyme converts glucose-6-phosphate into fructose-6-phosphate, which has the same atoms arranged differently. This shows that enzymes can:
o: Only add oxygen to a molecule
Rearrange atoms within a single molecule
questions.x: Besides splitting and joining molecules, some enzymes (isomerases) rearrange a molecule into an isomer with the same formula.

questions.q: Starch solution is mixed with saliva that was boiled and then cooled, and kept at 37 °C for 30 minutes. When tested with iodine, the mixture will:
o: Stay yellow-brown, because the starch has been digested
Stay yellow-brown, because boiling made the amylase more active
Turn blue-black, because the boiled amylase cannot digest the starch
Turn colourless, because the iodine is destroyed
questions.x: Boiling denatures salivary amylase permanently, so even after cooling the starch remains and gives the blue-black colour.

questions.q: Natural selection acts directly on an organism's:
o: Phenotype, the traits that are expressed
questions.x: The environment 'sees' the expressed traits (phenotype), such as colour or speed. Recessive alleles hidden in heterozygotes are not exposed to selection.

questions.q: In a snowy region, a rabbit population has some white and some brown individuals. Foxes spot the brown rabbits more easily. Over many generations:
o: Brown rabbits will turn white by trying to hide
The number of brown rabbits will increase
Fur colour will stay at the same ratio
White rabbits are expected to become more common
questions.x: White rabbits are camouflaged against snow, so more survive and breed, passing on the white colour. Individuals cannot change their inherited colour by effort.

questions.q: Darwin sailed on HMS Beagle in the role of the ship's:
questions.x: Darwin joined the Beagle as an unpaid naturalist. He collected plants, animals, fossils and rocks wherever the ship stopped.

questions.q: If the LH surge fails to occur in a cycle, which result is expected?
o: No ovulation, and so no corpus luteum forms
The corpus luteum persists for months
questions.x: The LH surge is the trigger for ovulation and for turning the follicle into a corpus luteum. Without it, the follicle does not release its oocyte.

questions.q: When progesterone falls at the end of a cycle, the coiled (spiral) arteries of the endometrium:
o: Grow longer to support an embryo
Constrict, cutting the blood supply so the lining breaks down
questions.x: Without progesterone, the spiral arteries constrict and the outer endometrium dies and is shed with blood as menstruation.

questions.q: HIV recognises and enters helper T cells by binding to which surface protein?
questions.x: The HIV envelope glycoprotein attaches to the CD4 receptor on helper T cells (and some other cells), so these are its main targets.

questions.q: In oogenesis, the first polar body is formed at the end of:
questions.x: Meiosis I in the primary oocyte divides the cytoplasm unequally, giving a large secondary oocyte and a small first polar body.

questions.q: In each half of a thick filament, the myosin molecules are arranged with:
o: Tails pointing toward the M line and heads pointing toward the Z line
Heads pointing toward the M line and tails toward the Z line
All heads gathered at the M line
Heads and tails lying in a random mix
questions.x: Myosin tails are bundled toward the centre (M line) and the heads project outward toward the Z lines. So the heads in each half pull the thin filaments of that half toward the centre.

questions.q: During long, continuous activity, which type of muscle tires (fatigues) most quickly?
o: All three tire at the same rate
questions.x: Skeletal muscle contracts quickly and powerfully but fatigues fast. Cardiac muscle works throughout life without fatigue, and smooth muscle can keep a slow contraction for a long time.

questions.q: Calcitonin lowers the blood calcium level mainly by:
o: Reducing bone resorption so that more calcium is deposited in bone
Increasing calcium absorption from the intestine
Releasing calcium stored in skeletal muscle
questions.x: Calcitonin from the thyroid gland inhibits osteoclasts and favours deposition of calcium in bone, so blood calcium falls. Stimulating osteoclasts would raise blood calcium.

questions.q: The specialised region of the sarcolemma lying under the axon terminal of a motor neuron, carrying acetylcholine receptors, is the:
questions.x: The motor end plate is the folded part of the muscle fibre membrane at the neuromuscular junction, rich in acetylcholine receptors. The synaptic knob belongs to the neuron, and nodes of Ranvier lie along myelinated axons.

questions.q: Each skeletal muscle fibre contains many nuclei because it:
o: Divides its nucleus repeatedly without ever forming fibres
Forms by the fusion of many embryonic cells (myoblasts)
Takes up nuclei from nearby nerve cells
Is made of many cells joined by intercalated discs
questions.x: During development many myoblasts fuse to form one long fibre, so the fibre ends up with many nuclei. Intercalated discs belong to cardiac muscle, whose cells stay separate.

questions.q: The end of a skeletal muscle that is attached to a bone which stays fixed during contraction is called the muscle's:
questions.x: The origin is the attachment to the bone that stays still. The insertion is the attachment to the bone that moves, and the belly is the thick, contracting middle part.

questions.q: Waves of contraction in the ureters, which push urine from the kidneys to the bladder, are produced by:
questions.x: Peristalsis in the ureters is produced by smooth muscle in their walls, working involuntarily.

questions.q: Cardiac muscle is described as striated. This means it:
o: Has only one nucleus in each cell
Shows alternating light and dark bands
questions.x: Striated means cross-banded: light and dark bands produced by the regular arrangement of actin and myosin filaments. Branching and single nuclei are separate features.

questions.q: After crossing over, a chromatid that carries a mix of maternal and paternal alleles is called a:
questions.x: A chromatid that took part in the exchange has a new combination of alleles and is recombinant. The chromatids not involved keep the parental combination.

questions.q: Genes on the part of the Y chromosome that has no matching part on the X are called:
questions.x: Genes found only on the Y are holandric (Y-linked) and are passed only from father to son. X-linked genes are on the X chromosome.

questions.q: With complete dominance for each gene, how many phenotypic classes are expected in the offspring of AaBbCc × AaBbCc?
questions.x: Each gene gives two phenotypes (dominant or recessive), so three genes give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 classes. 27 is the number of genotypes.

questions.q: In the cross AaBb × aaBb, with the genes assorting independently, what fraction of the offspring is expected to be aabb?
questions.x: Aa × aa gives aa with probability 1/2, and Bb × Bb gives bb with probability 1/4. Multiplying, 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8.

questions.q: A true-breeding round green line of peas is crossed with a true-breeding wrinkled yellow line. The hybrid seeds will be:
o: Round green and wrinkled yellow in equal numbers
questions.x: RRyy × rrYY gives only RrYy. Round and yellow are dominant, so all hybrid seeds are round yellow, a combination that neither parent showed.

questions.q: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes results in:
questions.x: Exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids gives new combinations of alleles, called recombination. It does not change the chromosome number.

questions.q: A student lists four facts about hemophilia. Which one is NOT correct?
o: Affected females are much rarer than affected males
It is caused by a recessive allele
A carrier woman passes the allele to about half her children
Its allele is carried on the Y chromosome
questions.x: The hemophilia allele is on the X chromosome, not the Y. The other statements are true of an X-linked recessive disorder.

questions.q: An organism carrying two identical alleles of a gene, such as TT or tt, is described as:
questions.x: Homozygous means both alleles of a gene are the same (TT or tt). A heterozygote or hybrid carries two different alleles (Tt); hemizygous means only one copy is present, as with X-linked genes in males.

questions.q: A doctor hears an extra swishing sound (a murmur) with the heartbeat. A common cause is:
o: A heart rate of 75 beats per minute
A heart valve that does not close properly, so blood leaks back
Normal closure of the semilunar valves
A very slow pulse at the wrist
questions.x: A murmur is an abnormal sound, often from blood leaking backwards through a faulty valve. Normal valve closure gives only the lubb and dubb sounds.

questions.q: Compared with the three-chambered heart of a frog, the four-chambered human heart:
o: Has only one atrium receiving all the blood
Keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood completely separate
Pumps blood through the body in a single circuit
Has no valves between atria and ventricles
questions.x: A complete septum and two ventricles keep oxygenated and deoxygenated blood fully apart in humans. A frog's single ventricle allows some mixing.

questions.q: Stroke volume is the:
o: Volume of blood pumped by both ventricles in one minute
Volume of blood pumped out by one ventricle in a single beat
Number of heartbeats in one minute
Volume of blood left in a ventricle after it contracts
questions.x: Stroke volume is the blood ejected by one ventricle per beat (about 70 mL at rest). Multiplying it by the heart rate gives cardiac output per minute.

questions.q: Which vessels return blood from the body's organs to the heart?
questions.x: Veins carry blood back towards the heart. Arteries and arterioles carry it away, and lacteals are lymph vessels.

questions.q: Which pairing of an immune cell with its role is correct?
o: Plasma cell — kills infected cells directly
Helper T cell — activates B cells and cytotoxic T cells
questions.x: Helper T cells coordinate the response by activating other lymphocytes. Plasma cells secrete antibodies, cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells, and histamine comes from mast cells.

questions.q: The first human disease to be wiped out worldwide by vaccination was:
questions.x: Smallpox was declared eradicated by the WHO in 1980 after a worldwide vaccination campaign. Polio, measles and tuberculosis still occur.

questions.q: Each B lymphocyte carries surface receptors that can bind:
o: Any antigen that enters the body
questions.x: Every B cell has many copies of one receptor, which fits one antigen only. That is why only a few B cells respond to any given antigen.

questions.q: A lung tumour grows into a bronchus and blocks it completely. The most direct result for the part of the lung supplied by that bronchus is that:
o: Its blood supply is cut off by the diaphragm
It produces more surfactant than normal
Air cannot reach its alveoli, so no gas exchange takes place there
questions.x: A blocked bronchus stops ventilation of the alveoli beyond it, so that region can no longer exchange gases; trapped mucus there also makes infection likely.

questions.q: Benzopyrene, a compound in the tar of tobacco smoke, is an example of a:
questions.x: Benzopyrene is one of the best-known cancer-causing chemicals (carcinogens) in tar. It damages DNA in the cells lining the airways.

questions.q: A person can hold a breath or speak a long sentence, overriding the normal breathing rhythm for a short time. This voluntary control comes from the:
questions.x: The automatic rhythm is set by the medulla, but the cerebral cortex can send voluntary impulses to the breathing muscles for a while. The cerebellum coordinates posture and movement, not voluntary breathing.

questions.q: Jaundice, a yellow colour of the skin and the whites of the eyes, develops when:
o: Too much bile is released into the duodenum
Bilirubin builds up in the blood, as when bile flow is blocked or the liver is diseased
The pancreas fails to secrete lipase
Too much glycogen is stored in the liver
questions.x: Bilirubin, a yellow bile pigment from broken-down haemoglobin, is normally removed by the liver in bile. If the liver is damaged or bile cannot drain, it accumulates in the blood and tissues.

questions.q: During swallowing, food is prevented from entering the nasal cavity because the:
o: Soft palate and uvula rise to close off the nasal passage
Hard palate moves down onto the tongue
questions.x: The soft palate with its uvula is raised to seal the passage to the nose. The epiglottis protects the windpipe, not the nasal cavity, and the hard palate is fixed bone that cannot move.

questions.q: A diet very high in common salt raises the risk of calcium stones mainly because:
o: Sodium chloride itself crystallises into stones
Salt makes the urine more dilute
Extra sodium excreted by the kidneys carries more calcium into the urine
Salt dissolves the lining of the ureter
questions.x: When the kidneys excrete more sodium they also excrete more calcium, so urine calcium rises. Sodium chloride is very soluble and does not form stones.

questions.q: Which combination of habits gives the greatest risk of calcium oxalate stones?
o: High fluid intake, low-oxalate diet, low-salt diet
Low fluid intake, high-oxalate diet, high-salt diet
High fluid intake, high-oxalate diet, low-salt diet
Low fluid intake, low-oxalate diet, low-salt diet
questions.x: Concentrated urine, extra oxalate and extra calcium excretion from high salt all push calcium oxalate towards crystallising.

questions.q: A transfusion of the wrong blood group can damage the kidneys because:
o: Antibodies in the donor blood dissolve the glomeruli
The donor blood contains extra urea
The donor plasma stops urine from forming in the bladder
Destroyed red cells release haemoglobin, which can block and damage the kidney tubules
questions.x: In a mismatched transfusion the red cells burst; the released haemoglobin is filtered and can clog and injure the tubules, causing acute kidney failure.

questions.q: The sudden, severe, wave-like pain felt when a stone is passing down the ureter is called:
questions.x: Renal colic is caused by the ureter contracting strongly against the stone. Angina is heart pain and heartburn comes from stomach acid.

questions.q: Kidney stones differ from gallstones in that kidney stones:
o: Form in the gall bladder and are mostly cholesterol
Form in the liver and are mostly bile pigments
Form in the urinary system and are mostly mineral salts
Form in the blood and are mostly proteins
questions.x: Kidney stones are crystals of salts such as calcium oxalate in the urinary tract. Cholesterol stones in the gall bladder are gallstones.

questions.q: In the urinary system, urine is formed in the:
questions.x: Urine is made by the nephrons of the kidneys. The ureters carry it, the bladder stores it and the urethra passes it out; none of these change it.

questions.q: Sodium ions are pumped out of the filtrate in the first coiled part of the nephron. Chloride ions there leave the filtrate mainly:
o: Not at all, so all the chloride ends up in urine
Passively, following the actively reabsorbed sodium ions
Only in the collecting duct, under ADH control
By being secreted back from the peritubular blood
questions.x: Sodium ions are pumped out of the PCT filtrate, and negatively charged chloride ions follow them passively; water then follows by osmosis. Most filtered chloride is therefore reclaimed.

questions.q: Which pair correctly names one substance that leaves the glomerular capillaries in the filtrate and one that leaves the peritubular capillaries by secretion into the tubule?
questions.x: Glucose is freely filtered, and hydrogen ions are secreted from peritubular blood into the tubule. Albumin and red cells are not filtered, and amino acids are reabsorbed rather than secreted.

questions.q: Aldosterone increases blood volume because:
o: Water follows the extra sodium ions reabsorbed, by osmosis
It makes the glomerulus filter less protein
It pumps water directly into the blood
It stimulates red blood cell production
questions.x: Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption in the DCT and collecting duct. Water follows the salt osmotically, so more water is kept in the blood and blood volume and pressure rise.

questions.q: A DNA probe with the sequence 5'-TACG-3' is used to detect an mRNA. The complementary mRNA sequence it pairs with is:
questions.x: T pairs with A, A with U (RNA has no T), C with G and G with C, and the strands run antiparallel. So the mRNA reads 3'-AUGC-5'. A sequence containing T cannot be mRNA.

questions.q: In blood banks, monoclonal antibodies are used to:
o: Destroy all bacteria in donated blood
Increase the number of red cells in stored blood
Copy the DNA of blood donors
Identify blood group antigens such as A, B and Rh accurately
questions.x: Monoclonal antibodies against the A, B and Rh antigens are highly specific and uniform, so they give reliable blood-grouping results. They do not sterilise blood or copy DNA.

questions.q: Streptomycin, an antibiotic used against tuberculosis, is obtained from:
questions.x: Streptomycin is produced by Streptomyces, a soil-dwelling bacterium that is a source of many antibiotics. Streptococcus is a pathogen and the source of streptokinase, not streptomycin.

questions.q: Bacteria can make a correct human protein such as insulin from an inserted human gene (cDNA) because:
o: Bacteria and humans have identical chromosomes
The genetic code is universal, so they translate the gene the same way
The human gene changes into a bacterial gene
questions.x: The same codons stand for the same amino acids in almost all organisms, so bacterial ribosomes produce the same amino acid sequence as human cells would from that gene.

questions.q: Copper reacts with dilute nitric acid: 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + 4H₂O. How many moles of HNO₃ are used for every mole of NO given off?
questions.x: The ratio HNO₃ : NO is 8 : 2 = 4 : 1, so 4 mol of HNO₃ are used per mole of NO. 2.67 is the ratio HNO₃ : Cu, and 0.25 is the inverted fraction.

questions.q: Sodium hydroxide neutralises sulphuric acid: 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. How many moles of NaOH neutralise 0.25 mol of H₂SO₄?
questions.x: The ratio NaOH : H₂SO₄ is 2 : 1, so 0.25 mol of acid needs 2 × 0.25 = 0.5 mol of NaOH. 0.125 mol comes from inverting the ratio.

questions.q: Within the same principal energy level of a many-electron atom, the energies of the sub-levels are in the order:
questions.x: In a many-electron atom, sub-levels of the same shell increase in energy as l increases: s < p < d < f. They are equal only in hydrogen.

questions.q: In Bohr's model, the energy of an electron in any orbit is given a negative value because:
o: Zero energy is taken at infinite distance, and energy is released as the electron is bound
The electron carries a negative charge
The electron loses energy continuously while moving
Energy is absorbed when the electron comes close to the nucleus
questions.x: A free electron at infinity is given zero energy. When it is attracted into an orbit, energy is given out, so its energy in the atom is below zero.

questions.q: In a vacuum, photons of X-rays and of visible light differ in frequency but have the same:
questions.x: All photons travel at the speed of light, 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, in a vacuum. Energy, wavelength and wave number all depend on frequency, so they differ.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a correct form of the ideal gas equation? (m = mass, M = molar mass, d = density)
questions.x: Volume increases with temperature, so T must be in the numerator: PV = nRT. Putting n = m/M gives PV = (m/M)RT, and using d = m/V gives PM = dRT.

questions.q: The absolute temperature of a fixed mass of gas is doubled at constant pressure. Its density:
questions.x: By Charles's law the volume doubles. The mass stays the same, so density (mass/volume) halves.

questions.q: A temperature of 400 K on the Celsius scale is:
questions.x: °C = K − 273, so 400 − 273 = 127 °C. Adding 273 instead gives the wrong 673 °C.

questions.q: The boiling points of the halogens increase in the order F₂ < Cl₂ < Br₂ < I₂ because:
o: Dipole–dipole forces grow stronger down the group
London dispersion forces grow stronger as molecular size and number of electrons increase
Hydrogen bonding grows stronger down the group
The covalent bond inside each molecule becomes stronger
questions.x: Halogen molecules are non-polar, so only London forces act; larger electron clouds are more polarisable. Boiling does not break the covalent bond inside the molecule.

questions.q: Ice floats on liquid water because:
o: Ice is denser than liquid water
Ice is less dense than liquid water
questions.x: Ice (about 0.92 g cm⁻³) is less dense than liquid water (about 1.00 g cm⁻³), so it floats. Its open hydrogen-bonded structure causes this.

questions.q: In rutile, TiO₂, each Ti⁴⁺ ion is surrounded by 6 O²⁻ ions. How many Ti⁴⁺ ions surround each O²⁻ ion?
questions.x: There are twice as many O²⁻ as Ti⁴⁺ ions, so the coordination number of O²⁻ is half that of Ti⁴⁺: 6/2 = 3.

questions.q: Which pair consists of two molecular crystals?
questions.x: Sucrose and iodine are both made of discrete molecules held by intermolecular forces. Diamond is a covalent network, and NaCl and MgO are ionic.

questions.q: The formation of ammonia, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, is:
o: Endothermic, ΔH ≈ +92 kJ for 2 mol NH₃
Exothermic, ΔH ≈ −46 kJ for 2 mol NH₃
Endothermic, ΔH ≈ +46 kJ for 2 mol NH₃
Exothermic, ΔH ≈ −92 kJ for 2 mol NH₃
questions.x: About 92 kJ of heat is given out per 2 mol of NH₃ (46 kJ per mole), so the reaction is exothermic. This is why high temperature lowers the yield.

questions.q: In the Haber process, nitrogen and hydrogen are fed to the converter in the volume ratio:
questions.x: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, so the gases are mixed in the ratio of the equation, 1 volume of N₂ to 3 volumes of H₂.

questions.q: 1 g of magnesium ribbon and 1 g of magnesium powder are each added to excess dilute HCl at the same temperature. Compared with the ribbon, the powder gives:
o: A faster initial rate and a larger total volume of hydrogen
A slower initial rate but the same total volume of hydrogen
The same initial rate but a larger total volume of hydrogen
A faster initial rate but the same total volume of hydrogen
questions.x: Powder has a larger surface area, so it reacts faster. The amount of magnesium is the same and the acid is in excess, so the final volume of H₂ is the same.

questions.q: The rate of a chemical reaction is defined as:
o: The total time taken for the reaction to finish
The amount of heat given out per mole of product
The change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time
The concentration of products at equilibrium
questions.x: Rate is how quickly concentration changes: Δ(concentration)/Δt, usually in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. The total time is not a rate.

questions.q: Food kept in a refrigerator goes bad more slowly than food left in a warm room because:
o: The reactions that cause decay are slower at lower temperature
Low temperature changes the products of decay
Cooling increases the activation energy of the reactions
questions.x: At lower temperature fewer particles have energy above Ea, so decay reactions slow down. Cooling does not change Ea itself.

questions.q: 200 cm³ of 0.5 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄ is fully neutralised by excess NaOH. Taking ΔH of neutralisation as −57 kJ per mole of water formed, how much heat is released?
questions.x: Moles of H₂SO₄ = 0.2 × 0.5 = 0.1, giving 0.2 mol H⁺ and so 0.2 mol H₂O. Heat = 0.2 × 57 = 11.4 kJ. Forgetting the two H⁺ gives 5.7 kJ.

questions.q: Heating a gas supplies 300 J to it, while the surroundings also compress it with 100 J of work. By how much does the internal energy of the gas change? (ΔE = q + w)
questions.x: q = +300 J and w = +100 J, so ΔE = 300 + 100 = +400 J. Both heat in and work on the system raise its internal energy.

questions.q: In the thermite reaction 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe, how many electrons are transferred as written?
questions.x: Each Al goes from 0 to +3, losing 3 electrons; 2 Al atoms lose 6. Likewise 2 Fe atoms each gain 3 electrons (+3 to 0), a total of 6.

questions.q: The half-reaction that takes place at the standard hydrogen electrode is:
questions.x: The SHE is a hydrogen/hydrogen-ion electrode; platinum is only an inert conductor and does not react.

questions.q: Which statement about a molecule that contains polar bonds is correct?
o: It may still be non-polar if its shape makes the bond dipoles cancel
It is non-polar only if it contains a lone pair
It is polar only if it is linear
questions.x: Polarity of a molecule depends on bond polarity and shape together. CO₂ and CCl₄ have polar bonds but are non-polar because their symmetrical shapes cancel the dipoles.

questions.q: Between two atoms, a pi (π) bond can form only when:
o: The atoms are of the same element
A sigma bond is already present between them
The atoms use s orbitals for bonding
No sigma bond is present between them
questions.x: A π bond never exists alone; the first bond between two atoms is always a σ bond, and π bonds are added in double and triple bonds.

questions.q: The H–Cl bond in hydrogen chloride is:
o: A pi bond formed by overlap of an s and a p orbital
A sigma bond formed by overlap of an s and a p orbital
A sigma bond formed by overlap of two s orbitals
A pi bond formed by sideways overlap of two p orbitals
questions.x: The 1s orbital of hydrogen overlaps head-on with a half-filled 3p orbital of chlorine, giving an s–p σ bond.

questions.q: Helium is placed with the noble gases in Group VIIIA (18), although its electronic configuration, 1s², is actually that of:
questions.x: Helium's last electron enters an s orbital, so by configuration it is s-block; it is placed with the noble gases because of its filled shell and inertness.

questions.q: Sodium and potassium are stored under kerosene (paraffin oil) because they:
o: React quickly with air and water
questions.x: Alkali metals react rapidly with oxygen and moisture, so they are kept under an unreactive oil.

questions.q: A first-row transition element has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d³ 4s². The element is:
questions.x: 18 + 3 + 2 = 23 electrons, so Z = 23, vanadium. Chromium has 24 electrons and is 3d⁵ 4s¹.

questions.q: Which compound is optically inactive?
questions.x: In glycine the central carbon carries two hydrogen atoms, so it is not chiral. Each of the others has a carbon bonded to four different groups.

questions.q: Which statement about the number of free radicals in each stage of a free-radical chain reaction is correct?
o: Initiation decreases it, propagation increases it, termination keeps it constant
Initiation increases it, propagation keeps it constant, termination decreases it
All three stages increase the number of radicals
Initiation and termination both increase it, while propagation decreases it
questions.x: Initiation splits a molecule into two radicals; each propagation step uses one radical and makes one; termination joins two radicals into a molecule.

questions.q: Alkanes are generally unreactive towards acids, bases and oxidising agents because:
o: Their carbon–carbon and carbon–hydrogen bonds are strong and almost non-polar, and they have no π electrons
Their carbon atoms are sp² hybridised
They have lone pairs that repel reagents
questions.x: With strong, nearly non-polar σ bonds and no π electrons, alkanes offer no site for polar reagents to attack. They react mainly by free-radical substitution.

questions.q: Which alkyl halide can NOT give an alkene by dehydrohalogenation?
questions.x: Elimination needs a hydrogen on the carbon next to the one carrying the halogen. CH₃Cl has only one carbon, so there is no such hydrogen and no alkene can form.

questions.q: Nitrobenzene is sulphonated with fuming sulphuric acid. The main product is:
questions.x: The –NO₂ group is a meta-director, so the –SO₃H group enters position 3.

questions.q: But-1-yne, CH≡CCH₂CH₃, is hydrated with dilute H₂SO₄ and HgSO₄. The final product is:
questions.x: Water adds by Markovnikov's rule to give an enol with –OH on C2, which rearranges to the ketone CH₃COCH₂CH₃ (butanone). Only ethyne gives an aldehyde.

questions.q: Number the longest chain in CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ so that the branches get the lowest locants. The resulting systematic name is:
questions.x: The longest chain is five carbons, with methyl groups on carbons 2 and 3 when numbered from the left. Numbering from the right would give the higher locants 3,4.

questions.q: What volume of chlorine at STP is needed to convert 0.1 mol of methane completely into dichloromethane?
questions.x: CH₄ + 2Cl₂ → CH₂Cl₂ + 2HCl, so 0.1 mol CH₄ needs 0.2 mol Cl₂; 0.2 × 22.4 = 4.48 dm³. Using a 1 : 1 ratio gives the wrong 2.24 dm³.

questions.q: Which hydrocarbon reacts with sodium metal to give hydrogen gas?
questions.x: Only the ≡C–H hydrogen of ethyne is acidic enough to be replaced by sodium, forming sodium acetylide and H₂.

questions.q: Tertiary alkyl halides such as (CH₃)₃CBr react extremely slowly by the SN2 mechanism because:
o: The C–Br bond in them is too strong to break
The bulky methyl groups block attack from the back of the carbon
They have no hydrogen on the β-carbon
questions.x: SN2 needs the nucleophile to approach from the side opposite the halogen, and three alkyl groups crowd that side (steric hindrance). Tertiary carbocations are in fact the most stable.

questions.q: Ethanol is heated with concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 140 °C, with the alcohol in excess. The main organic product is:
questions.x: At about 140 °C with excess ethanol, two molecules lose one water molecule between them: 2C₂H₅OH → C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + H₂O. At about 170 °C with excess acid, ethene forms instead.

questions.q: When an alcohol is dehydrated by concentrated H₂SO₄, the first step is:
o: Loss of a hydride ion from the –OH carbon
Attack of HSO₄⁻ on the oxygen atom
Protonation of the oxygen of the –OH group by H⁺
Removal of the O–H hydrogen as H⁺ by the acid
questions.x: The acid protonates the –OH oxygen, turning it into –OH₂⁺, which leaves as a water molecule, a far better leaving group than OH⁻. Here the alcohol acts as a base, not an acid.

questions.q: In reactions of the carbonyl group, an electrophile such as H⁺ attaches to:
o: A hydrogen atom of the alkyl group
questions.x: The oxygen is δ− and carries lone pairs, so electrophiles such as H⁺ bond to it. Nucleophiles attack the δ+ carbonyl carbon.

questions.q: Butyraldehyde, CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO, has the systematic (IUPAC) name:
questions.x: The –CHO group is always on C-1 of the chain, so the four-carbon aldehyde is simply butanal; no position number is needed. A ketone can never be on C-1.

questions.q: In the carbonyl group of an aldehyde, the partial charges are:
questions.x: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so it pulls the bonding electrons towards itself and becomes δ−, leaving the carbon δ+.

questions.q: A chlorine atom is attached to the carbon farthest from the carboxyl group in ClCH₂CH₂COOH. Its systematic name is:
questions.x: Numbering starts at the carboxyl carbon (C-1), so the chlorine is on C-3 of a three-carbon acid.

questions.q: A protein that gives only α-amino acids on complete hydrolysis is classified as a:
questions.x: Simple proteins such as albumin are made of amino acids alone. A conjugated protein (for example a nucleoprotein) also gives a non-protein part on hydrolysis.

questions.q: A dye differs from a pigment in that a dye:
o: Is insoluble and only coats the surface with a binder
Is usually soluble in the dyeing medium and becomes attached to the fibre
Has no chromophore in its molecule
questions.x: Dyes are applied from solution and are taken up by or bound to the fibre. Pigments are insoluble particles held on the surface by a binder, as in paints.

questions.q: Vector P = 2î + aĵ and vector Q = 3î − 2ĵ are perpendicular to each other. The value of a is:
questions.x: Perpendicular vectors have P · Q = 0: 2 × 3 + a × (−2) = 0, so 6 − 2a = 0 and a = 3.

questions.q: Variable (non-uniform) acceleration is present when, in equal time intervals, the velocity of a body:
o: Changes by equal amounts in equal intervals of time
Changes by unequal amounts in equal intervals of time
questions.x: Variable (non-uniform) acceleration means the rate of change of velocity is not constant, so the velocity changes by different amounts in equal time intervals.

questions.q: A ball hits a wall at 10 m s⁻¹ and rebounds along the same line at 8 m s⁻¹. The contact lasts 0.1 s. The magnitude of its average acceleration during contact is:
questions.x: Velocity reverses, so the change is 8 − (−10) = 18 m s⁻¹. a = 18 ÷ 0.1 = 180 m s⁻². 20 m s⁻² ignores the change of direction.

questions.q: A ball rolls off a horizontal table top at 4 m s⁻¹. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², after how long will its speed be 5 m s⁻¹?
questions.x: Horizontal component stays 4 m s⁻¹, so the vertical component must be √(25 − 16) = 3 m s⁻¹. t = 3 ÷ 10 = 0.3 s.

questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 20 m s⁻¹. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², the time it takes to reach its highest point is:
questions.x: At the top v = 0, so 0 = 20 − 10t and t = 2 s. 4 s is the total time to go up and come back down.

questions.q: Blocks of 4 kg and 6 kg are in contact on a smooth horizontal surface. A horizontal force of 20 N pushes the 4 kg block, which in turn pushes the 6 kg block. The force between the blocks is:
questions.x: Both move together: a = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 m s⁻². The only horizontal force on the 6 kg block is the contact force, so it is 6 × 2 = 12 N. 8 N is the net force on the 4 kg block.

questions.q: A raindrop falls at a constant (terminal) velocity. According to Newton's first law, this means that:
o: No force acts on the drop
The air resistance is greater than its weight
The air resistance on the drop is equal to its weight
questions.x: Constant velocity means zero net force, so the upward air resistance exactly balances the downward weight. Both forces still act.

questions.q: A force vector F = (3i + 4j) N moves a body through a displacement vector d = (2i + j) m. The work done is:
questions.x: W = F·d = (3)(2) + (4)(1) = 6 + 4 = 10 J. Work is the scalar product, so matching components are multiplied and added.

questions.q: Taking the ground as zero, a 1 kg bucket in a well is lowered from a depth of 2 m to a depth of 4 m. Its potential energy changes by (g = 10 m s⁻²):
questions.x: PE changes from −20 J to −40 J, so ΔPE = −40 − (−20) = −20 J. The bucket went down, so its PE decreased.

questions.q: Taking 1 rad ≈ 57.3°, an angle of 0.5 rad is approximately:
questions.x: 0.5 × 57.3° ≈ 28.6°. Doubling instead of halving gives 114.6°.

questions.q: A point on the rim of a pulley of radius 0.2 m moves at 6 m s⁻¹. The angular speed of the pulley is:
questions.x: ω = v/r = 6/0.2 = 30 rad s⁻¹. Multiplying v by r gives 1.2, which is wrong.

questions.q: The quantity ½ρv² for a moving fluid is physically equal to its:
o: Kinetic energy per unit mass of the fluid
Kinetic energy per unit volume of the fluid
Potential energy per unit volume of the fluid
questions.x: ½mv² divided by the volume V gives ½(m/V)v² = ½ρv², the kinetic energy per unit volume.

questions.q: An ideal (non-viscous) fluid flows at constant speed through a horizontal pipe of uniform cross-section. No pressure difference is needed between the ends to keep it flowing because:
o: The fluid is compressed as it flows
There is no internal friction to overcome
questions.x: With no viscosity there is no friction to work against, so no net force (and so no pressure difference) is needed to keep the fluid moving at constant speed. A real viscous fluid would need one.

questions.q: In the steady flow of an incompressible fluid through a pipe, which quantities at a FIXED point in the pipe remain constant with time?
o: Only the velocity; the density may change
Both the fluid's velocity and its density
Only the density; the velocity may change
Neither the velocity nor the density
questions.x: Steady flow keeps the velocity at each point constant in time, and incompressible flow keeps the density constant. Together, both are constant at any fixed point.

questions.q: When two coherent waves superpose, whether the result at a point is a maximum or a minimum depends on:
o: The speed of the waves only
The phase difference between the waves at that point
The direction in which the observer faces
questions.x: In phase (0, 2π, ...) gives a maximum and opposite phase (π, 3π, ...) gives a minimum. The phase difference at each point fixes the type of interference there.

questions.q: Two musicians tune their instruments by playing the same note together and listening for beats. The instruments are in tune when:
o: The beats are as fast as possible
Exactly one beat is heard every second
The sound becomes twice as loud at every moment
questions.x: The beat frequency equals the difference of the two frequencies. When the beats vanish, the difference is zero, so the notes match.

questions.q: A guitarist presses a string against a fret, shortening its vibrating length while the tension stays the same. The note produced:
o: Has the same frequency but is louder
Has the same frequency but a longer wavelength in air
questions.x: The fundamental frequency is v/2L, and the wave speed on the string is unchanged. A shorter length L therefore gives a higher frequency.

questions.q: Mechanical waves cannot travel through a vacuum because they travel by:
o: Changes in electric and magnetic fields
Vibrations of particles that pass the disturbance on to their neighbours
A flow of matter from the source to the receiver
Heat passing from hot regions to cold regions
questions.x: A mechanical wave is passed along by particles of the medium pushing and pulling on neighbouring particles. A vacuum has no particles, so the wave cannot be passed on.

questions.q: A tuning fork of 512 Hz sounded with a second fork gives 6 beats per second. The frequency of the second fork could be:
questions.x: Beat frequency = |f₁ − f₂|, so the second fork is 6 Hz above or below 512 Hz. Halving the difference to 3 Hz is a common mistake.

questions.q: A sound is made outdoors on a hot afternoon and again at dawn, when the air is cooler. Other conditions being equal, the sound travels faster:
o: In the hot afternoon, because the air temperature is higher
At dawn, because cool air is denser
At the same speed both times
At dawn, because sound carries better in still air
questions.x: The speed of sound in air increases with temperature (v ∝ √T in kelvin), so it is faster in the warmer afternoon air.

questions.q: A body in SHM passes through its equilibrium (mean) position. At that moment:
o: Its speed is maximum and its acceleration is zero
Its speed is zero and its acceleration is maximum
Both its speed and its acceleration are maximum
Both its speed and its acceleration are zero
questions.x: At the mean position the displacement is zero, so the acceleration (∝ displacement) is zero, while all the energy is kinetic, so the speed is maximum.

questions.q: Two substances have the same specific heat but different molar masses. Their molar specific heats are:
o: In the inverse ratio of their molar masses
In the same ratio as their molar masses
questions.x: Molar specific heat C = Mc. With the same c, C is proportional to the molar mass M.

questions.q: Half a mole of water (18 g per mole) is warmed through 10 K. If water needs 4.2 kJ per kg per kelvin, the energy required is:
questions.x: Mass = 0.5 × 0.018 = 0.009 kg. Q = 0.009 × 4200 × 10 = 378 J. Taking 1 mol (0.018 kg) gives 756 J; treating 0.5 mol as 0.5 kg gives 21 000 J.

questions.q: A small positive charge is released from rest in a uniform electric field. Ignoring gravity, it moves:
o: Along the direction of the field, at constant speed
Opposite to the direction of the field, with increasing speed
At right angles to the field, at constant speed
Along the direction of the field, with steadily increasing speed
questions.x: A uniform field exerts a constant force qE in the field direction on a positive charge, so it accelerates uniformly along the field.

questions.q: Three equal positive charges are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle. The net electric field at the centre of the triangle is:
o: Three times the field due to one charge
Twice the field due to one charge
Directed towards one of the corners
questions.x: The centre is equidistant from all three charges, and the three equal fields point at 120° to each other, so their vector sum is zero.

questions.q: Electric field lines meet the surface of a charged conductor at rest:
o: At right angles to the surface
questions.x: In electrostatics a conductor's surface has no field component along it, so the field lines are perpendicular to the surface where they meet it.

questions.q: Resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω are joined in series across a 20 V supply of negligible internal resistance. The potential difference across the 6 Ω resistor is:
questions.x: Total resistance = 10 Ω, so I = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 A. V across 6 Ω = 2 × 6 = 12 V; the 4 Ω resistor takes the other 8 V.

questions.q: An 18 V battery (no internal resistance) feeds a network: a 6 Ω resistor followed by a pair of 6 Ω resistors joined side by side. How much current leaves the battery?
questions.x: The parallel pair is 3 Ω, so the total is 3 + 6 = 9 Ω. I = 18 ÷ 9 = 2 A. Adding all three as 18 Ω gives 1 A.

questions.q: A uniform field B passes through a flat area A whose normal makes an angle θ with B. The magnetic flux through the area is:
questions.x: Φ = B · A = BA cos θ, where θ is the angle between B and the normal (vector area). It is BA when the field is along the normal.

questions.q: A copper plate swinging between the poles of a strong magnet comes to rest much sooner than one swinging outside the field. This is because:
o: Air resistance is larger between the poles
Eddy currents induced in the plate oppose its motion
questions.x: The moving plate cuts the field, inducing eddy currents. By Lenz's law these oppose the motion, damping the swing. Copper is not attracted by a magnet.

questions.q: In a transformer, the coil that is connected to the alternating supply is called the:
questions.x: The input coil connected to the AC supply is the primary; the output coil connected to the load is the secondary.

questions.q: An electromagnetic wave consists of:
o: Electric and magnetic fields oscillating along the direction of travel
Particles of matter vibrating in a medium
Electric and magnetic fields oscillating at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel
A magnetic field alone, oscillating at right angles to its motion
questions.x: EM waves are transverse: the electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation, and need no medium.

questions.q: A diode can be used for rectification because it has:
o: High resistance in forward bias and low resistance in reverse bias
Low resistance in forward bias and very high resistance in reverse bias
The same low resistance in both directions
The same high resistance in both directions
questions.x: Rectification needs a one-way device. A diode conducts easily in forward bias but almost blocks current in reverse bias.

questions.q: The scientist who explained the photoelectric effect by treating light as a stream of photons was:
questions.x: Einstein (1905) applied Planck's quantum idea to light itself, explaining the threshold frequency and his photoelectric equation hf = φ + KEmax.

questions.q: Lead-214 (²¹⁴₈₂Pb) emits a beta particle, then another beta particle, then an alpha particle. The final nucleus is:
questions.x: Two beta decays raise Z by 2 (82 → 84) with A unchanged; the alpha decay then lowers A by 4 and Z by 2, giving A = 210, Z = 82.

questions.q: An isotope has a decay constant of 0.231 per hour. Its half-life is:
questions.x: T½ = 0.693/λ = 0.693/0.231 = 3 hours. Multiplying instead of dividing gives about 0.16.

questions.q: The surgeon's face was grave as he came out of the operating theatre. He took off his mask slowly, asked the family to sit down, and spoke in a low voice about the next forty-eight hours. Hamza's mother held his hand tightly. As used in the passage, 'grave' means:
questions.x: Here 'grave' is an adjective describing a face: his low voice and the family's fear show it means serious. 'Burial place' is the meaning of the noun 'grave', which does not fit this sentence.

questions.q: "Cracks had made the old footbridge so precarious that engineers closed it to everyone until repairs were done." The word 'precarious' means:
questions.x: 'Precarious' means unsafe and likely to fall or fail; cracks and its closure for safety show this.

questions.q: Which sentence has an UNCLEAR pronoun reference?
o: Ali told Sara that she had won the prize.
Ali told Hamza that he had won the prize.
Ali said that he had won the prize.
Ayesha told Hamza that he had won the prize.
questions.x: In the first sentence 'he' could mean Ali or Hamza; in the others only one possible antecedent matches the pronoun.

questions.q: Choose the correct form: "I suggest ___ early tomorrow to avoid the traffic."
questions.x: 'Suggest' is followed by a gerund (or a that-clause), never by a to-infinitive.

questions.q: Pick the sentence in which the verb after 'avoided' is in the right form.
o: She avoided to answer the question.
She avoided to answering the question.
questions.x: 'Avoid' is always followed by a gerund (-ing form), never by a to-infinitive or a bare verb.

questions.q: Choose the correct pronoun: "Either the twins or Ali will lend you ___ bicycle."
questions.x: With 'either ... or', the pronoun agrees with the nearer antecedent, which is the singular 'Ali', so 'his' is correct.

questions.q: In "The tea is too hot to drink", the word 'too' is an adverb of:
questions.x: Adverbs of degree tell how much; 'too' tells the degree of heat.

questions.q: Identify the error in this sentence: "Bilal has been absent from college since three days."
o: 'since three days' should be 'for three days'
questions.x: 'For' is used with a length of time (three days); 'since' is used with a point in time (Monday, 2020). 'Absent from' is the correct preposition.

questions.q: Which option correctly corrects the comma splice in "The shop was closed, we went home."?
o: The shop was closed, we so went home.
The shop was closed, so we went home.
The shop was closed, and so went home.
The shop being closed, so we went home.
questions.x: Two main clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone; adding the conjunction 'so' after the comma fixes it. 'And so went home' has lost its subject, and 'being closed, so' mixes two structures.

questions.q: Three different whole numbers, each greater than 1, add up to 10. Which statement must be true?
questions.x: The only set of three different whole numbers above 1 with a sum of 10 is 2, 3 and 5. So one number must be 5; none is 4 or 6, and 2 is even.

questions.q: Saad says: "If we allow students one late submission, soon nobody will submit anything on time and the college will collapse." Which error in reasoning is this?
questions.x: Saad claims that one small step will lead to a chain of extreme results without showing why each step must follow. That is a slippery slope.

questions.q: Find the next number: 1024, 256, 64, 16, ?
questions.x: Each term is the one before divided by 4: 16 / 4 = 4.

questions.q: A building has six floors numbered 1 (lowest) to 6. Rafay, Sadia, Tariq, Umer, Vania and Wajid each live on a different floor. Rafay lives on floor 4. Sadia lives two floors above Rafay, and Tariq directly below Rafay. Umer lives on an odd-numbered floor below Tariq. Wajid does not live next to Sadia. Who lives on floor 5?
questions.x: Rafay 4, Sadia 6, Tariq 3, and Umer 1 (the only odd floor below 3). Floors 2 and 5 are left; Wajid cannot be next to Sadia, so he is on 2 and Vania on 5.

questions.q: Ayesha thinks of a two-digit number. Its digits add up to 11, and its tens digit is 3 more than its units digit. What is the number?
questions.x: Tens + units = 11 and tens - units = 3, so tens = 7 and units = 4: the number is 74. 47 has the digits the wrong way round.

questions.q: Statement: A city hospital's emergency ward is overloaded because nearby districts have no emergency facilities. Courses of action: I. Emergency facilities should be set up in the district hospitals. II. The city hospital should refuse patients from other districts. III. The city hospital's emergency ward should be expanded meanwhile. Which course(s) of action follow?
o: I, II and III all follow
questions.x: Action I removes the root cause and action III handles the load until then. Refusing emergency patients would put lives at risk, so II does not follow.

questions.q: Statement: A school's results improved after it began holding short weekly tests. Courses of action: I. The school should stop all teaching and only hold tests. II. The school should continue the weekly tests. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: The information shows the weekly tests help, so continuing them is sensible. Tests cannot replace teaching, so action I does not follow.

questions.q: Statement I: Many flights at Islamabad airport were delayed on Tuesday morning because pilots could not see the runway clearly. Statement II: Traffic on the motorway near Islamabad moved very slowly on Tuesday morning because drivers could hardly see the road. Which of the following is correct?
o: Both statements are effects of some common cause
Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
questions.x: Flight delays do not slow motorway traffic, nor the other way round. Both statements point to the same poor visibility that morning, such as thick fog, so they are effects of a common cause.

questions.q: Statement I: Most students in a college improved their biology marks this term after a new biology teacher joined. Statement II: Most students in the same college improved their chemistry marks this term after the chemistry laboratory was fully re-equipped. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
questions.x: Better biology marks do not cause better chemistry marks, or the reverse. Each improvement follows its own separate cause (a new teacher, a re-equipped laboratory), so they are effects of independent causes.
